entries.title: Israel election: Exit polls show no clear winner, with Netanyahu's fate unclear
entries.summary: While Netanyahu's party is projected to be the biggest in parliament, two out of three exit polls show his bloc even with the opposition. No bloc has a clear majority. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Israel

Israel election: Exit polls show no clear winner

Published October 27, 2026last updated October 28, 2026

While Netanyahu's party is projected to be the biggest in parliament, two out of three exit polls show his bloc even with the opposition. No bloc has a clear majority. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Israelis have voted, at a high turnout, in a parliamentary election that appears to have produced no clear winner
  • The pro-Netanyahu bloc and anti-Netanyahu bloc each have 51 seats, according to public broadcaster KAN
  • Two Arab parties have gained 18 seats between them
  • At least 61 seats are needed to form a secure majority
  • Israel election committee reports highest voter turnout on record as of 2 p.m., halfway through the voting day
  • Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, faces a staunch challenge to his grip on power
  • His chief rival is former military chief Gadi Eisenkot
  • Eisenkot called on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech
  • Netanyahu, meanwhile, called for a 'strong' right-wing government and said his Likud party is the biggest

Follow below for all the latest on the Israeli election on October 27, 2026, and its aftermath:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election

Netanyahu calls for 'strong' right-wing government after election

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has vowed to form a new right-wing government, despite exit polls showing no clear majority for either political bloc.

"We are still waiting for the real results," Netanyahu told cheering supporters in a speech early Wednesday, stressing that his Likud party was the largest in Israel.

"We must put in place a strong government of the right," he said.

Netanyahu also rejected the prospect of a government relying on the support of Arab parties, which made strong gains in Tuesday's election.

Turning to security, Netanyahu said Israel had a "unique opportunity" together with US President Donald Trump to end what he called the Iranian threat.

Updated exit polls show Netanyahu's bloc and the opposition led by Gadi Eisenkot either tied or separated by a narrow margin. Neither side is projected to win the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset.

Skip next section Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck

Updated exit polls show Netanyahu and opposition blocs neck and neck

Updated Israeli exit polls suggest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc is now tied with the opposition, after earlier projections showed a narrow lead for the bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot.

Public broadcaster Kan 11 and Channel 13 both put the pro-Netanyahu and anti-Netanyahu blocs at 51 seats each. Channel 12, meanwhile, is now showing the pro-Netanyahu camp with an edge at 52 seats and the opposition at 49 seats.

Kan 11's latest projection gives Netanyahu's Likud party 27 seats, up from 25 in its earlier poll.

However, none of the three major networks project either bloc winning the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament, the Knesset.

Skip next section Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech

Eisenkot calls on Netanyahu to resign in post-election speech

Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has called on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step down, saying voters have sent a clear message that they want change.

"We've made history," Eisenkot told supporters in a speech in Jerusalem following Tuesday's election. "The public voted against the continuation of Netanyahu as prime minister."

He said a "decent leader" would accept the public's will and announce his resignation, warning that another round of elections would be a mistake.

Eisenkot pledged to work towards forming what he called a "Zionist conscription government," referring to his push for broader military service obligations.

"We would like to represent all Israelis," he said, adding that the country needed stable leadership and a government that represented all parts of society.

The former military chief also warned Netanyahu against making major security decisions or launching new wars, arguing that he no longer had a mandate to do so.

"Netanyahu: Don't you dare use Israel's security for your political needs," Eisenkot said.

Skip next section Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government

Eisenkot says he is ready to form a government

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, said the election results pointed to a "complete lack of confidence" in Netanyahu and his coalition.

"I will act immediately to carry out the people’s mandate, replace Netanyahu's government and form a Zionist government committed to military conscription as soon as possible," Eisenkot said in a statement.

A former military chief, he made the issue of eliminating exemptions from military service for Ultra-Orthodox men central to his campaign.

Skip next section Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show

Majority of Israeli public voted against Netanyahu, exit polls show

Much of the Israeli media labeled the Israeli election an opinion poll on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

If the exit polls of Israel's main news outlets are anything to go by, the Israeli public voted against the country's longest-serving prime minister.

While Netanyahu's current coalition includes 68 seats, the exit polls gave his bloc between 50 and 51 seats.

The Israeli prime minister is unlikely to concede defeat despite his coalition having taken a significant hit, but it remains to be seen how Likud's own ranks, as well as its coalition partners, will react to the exit polls.

Skip next section Ra'am party becomes political power broker

Ra'am party becomes political power broker

The success of Ra'am, which exit polls predict will take seven seats, means no Israeli government can be established without the religious Muslim party playing some part.

The party already made headlines after appointing Yoav Segalovich, a Jewish former high-ranking police chief, as the number two candidate to leader Mansour Abbas. The raging criminality and violence across the Arab and Palestinian community, as well as the war in Gaza, both could have played a role in Ra'am's result.

Both the Likud-led coalition and large parts of the Israeli opposition may have ruled out a coalition with Ra'am, but the current results may leave them little choice but to seek some form of cooperation with the party.

As one Israeli pollster put it, "Tonight, Israelis were reminded that their population also includes Arabs and Palestinians with Israeli citizenship."

Skip next section Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say

Netanyahu's bloc trails in Israel election, exit polls say

Exit polls from Israel's major television networks project that a majority of Israelis voted against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition, but his Likud party has emerged as the largest single group in the Knesset, with 25 projected seats.

Challenger Gadi Eisenkot's bloc has emerged as the largest group with a projected 53, just ahead of the ruling coalition on 50, but well short of the 61 needed for a majority.

Neither bloc has a clear majority without the support of Arab parties.

These projected numbers are from public broadcaster Kan 11; other numbers vary by channel, but only slightly.

Skip next section Polls closing around the country

Polls closing around the country

It's now 10 p.m. across Israel, which means that polling stations around the country either should have closed or should be making preparations to do so as the last people in line cast their ballots.

Exit polls should follow shortly on Israeli television. These have a fairly good reputation overall but of course are only projections.

Results will start to trickle in through the night and are unlikely to be finalized until Wednesday.

And of course, there's every chance that even once the dust has settled and the final results are in, we will have a longer wait until there's clarity about who might be able to form a coalition government.

In any case, stick with us and we'll keep you posted.

Skip next section Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request

Election commission sees 'no need to extend voting hours' after Netanyahu request

The Central Elections Committee has rejected a request by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and some other groups to extend voting beyond 10 p.m. (2000 UTC/GMT).

"High nationwide turnout across all sectors of society reflects strong public engagement in the democratic process, and no need to extend voting hours was identified," a commission statement said.

The committee noted, however, that this decision was based on the circumstances "as things stand," leaving open the possibility for matters to change.

For instance, voting hours have been extended in some areas, including a polling location used by Israeli settlers in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, where a power outage led to an extension of the closing time from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Polling stations with fewer than 350 eligible voters typically close two hours earlier than larger polling stations in urban areas.

The commission has also said several times that anybody who started queueing before closing time will be given a chance to vote.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign

IN DEPTH: How AI reshaped Israel's election campaign

Artificial intelligence is emerging as a major factor in Israel's election campaign, with political parties using AI-generated videos, automated calls and online content on a large scale.

DW's Josh Axelrod examined the growing role of AI in the campaign, as researchers and analysts raise concerns about misleading content, bots and deepfakes ahead of the vote.

Skip next section High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc

High turnout could spell problems for Netanyahu's bloc

The expected high turnout means the number of votes needed to cross the 3.25% threshold to enter the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, is going to be higher, meaning smaller parties are at risk of not making it.

According to opinion polls from last week, the two parties that are on the threshold limit are Amcha Israel, a far-right party led by former military commander Ofer Winter, and the Reservists Party, which has not declared support for either main bloc.

Winter repeatedly said he intends to join a Netanyahu coalition, and a scenario in which his party doesn't make it to parliament puts Likud's chances of a future coalition at risk.

Either way, Israel's Central Elections Committee will have to make a decision on the matter within the hour.

Skip next section Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.

Turnout reaches 2 in 3 voters by 6 p.m.

Voter turnout reached 66.7%, or roughly two in every three eligible voters, by 6 p.m. local time, according to an update from the Central Elections Committee.

This remains the highest partial turnout figure since such records were first taken in 1973.

The level is only slightly clear of the previous high of 65.2% in 1973 and 1988 — but it quite considerably surpasses the 57.7% who had voted by this time in 2022.

And that figure had already been the highest 6 p.m. turnout of the 21st century before being surpassed today.

Skip next section WATCH: Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel’s election?

WATCH: Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel’s election?

Arab voters could play a decisive role in Israel's election. With neither Benjamin Netanyahu nor Gadi Eisenkot expected to win a Knesset majority, Arab parties could become key to forming the next government.

Activists worked to boost voter turnout, especially among young voters.

Skip next section Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters

Netanyahu emphasizes Arab turnout in appeals to his own voters

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continued issuing appeals to supporters to go out and vote online as the day progressed. 

One common theme was apparent in almost all of the posts: warnings about high turnout in Arab and to a lesser extent left-leaning communities.

"We're at war for our home," one of Netanyahu's posts read, using a phrase that appeared repeatedly in his messaging. "Muslim Brotherhood supporters are raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections. Go out and vote, recover it!!"

In another post he showed an image claiming to show a long line of voters queueing in Rahat, with a crowd of women wearing niqab coverings prominently visible at the front of the queue, suggesting that they were Muslim Palestinian voters.

Sami Abou Shahadeh, the leader of the Balad party, which is part of the alliance known as the Joint List, in turn called on his supporters to vote before the deadline expired, also highlighting similar appeals to voters from the leader of the far-right Jewish Power party, Itamar Ben-Gvir.

"There is one response to the incitement by Ben-Gvir and Netanyahu against the Arab citizens that has been going on all day: go out and vote for the Joint List!" he wrote.

Skip next section President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel'

President of German-Israeli Society, Volker Beck, says a change would be 'good for Israel'

The president of the German-Israeli Society, Green party politician Volker Beck, said in a TV interview on election day that he believed a change in leadership might be in Israel's interests.

"It would be good for Israel, if it were to come to a change, because I believe that [Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu has squandered a great deal of trust in recent years, both in foreign and domestic policy," Beck said in an interview broadcast on sister channels RTL and ntv.

Beck, a Bundestag lawmaker for more than two decades with the Greens who was perhaps best known as a politician as a campaigner for LGBT rights and advocate of an uncompromising Israeli foreign policy, is not typically associated with stern criticism of Netanyahu or his government. 

"Although he has also done some things right and has done some necessary things, a change is really needed" to allow Israel to recoup support among the international community, Beck said, as Netanyahu becomes an increasingly polarizing figure on the world stage.

He also criticized domestic efforts by the Likud-led government to reform the legal system and its influence over politics, saying this would "fundamentally change Israel's character, and should be stopped."

Beck said he hoped that a functioning majority would emerge from the vote, but acknowledged that pollsters anticipated a stalemate. In that scenario, he said, he would personally favor a national unity government incorporating all the major players.

But at present he thought the "divide between the two camps is so deep, that it really would be a bit of a masterstroke to be able to bring them together." He made a similar comment online, saying such a unity govermment "would be good" but was "not very likely."

entries.title: Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate
entries.summary: Heat, drought and storms linked to climate change are already killing millions worldwide. Researchers want global warming to be declared a global health emergency as the health harms from it escalate faster than ever.
entries.content:
ClimateGlobal issues

Experts urge 'global health emergency' as climate harms accelerate

October 28, 2026

Heat, drought and storms linked to climate change are already killing millions worldwide. Researchers want global warming to be declared a global health emergency as the health harms from it escalate faster than ever.

As heat deaths, drought and food insecurity accelerate worldwide, nearly 150 researchers from more than 30 countries are calling for climate change to be declared a "global health emergency." 

The health and economic toll of planetary heating has risen sharply in the decade since countries signed the Paris climate accord — a landmark deal to stop climate change that was hailed by the World Health Organization (WHO) at the time as "the most important public health agreement of the century."

Yet, climate change was responsible for more than half a million heat deaths in 2023 alone and nearly 3 million since 2016. The area affected by extreme drought, which threatens food and water supplies and raises the risk of disease, grew more than 700% faster than in the decade before. And heat cost the world an estimated $1.07 trillion in lost potential income last year, all according to the annual Lancet Countdown on Health and Climate Change.

"This cannot continue," said Alan Dangour, director of climate and health at Wellcome Trust, one of the world's largest charities, which funded the Lancet report. "We must change course and put the health and well-being of people at the heart of our response to climate change — measuring success not through emissions targets or degrees Celsius but by lives saved and health outcomes improved."

Climate-linked health harms growing faster than before

The latest findings from the Lancet study show how rapidly the health risks are growing by comparing this decade to the one before the Paris Agreement was signed.

Heat is the starkest example. Climate change was responsible for 68% of heat-related deaths between 2016 and 2023, up from 55% in the previous decade. The yearly increase in climate-driven heat deaths more than doubled over the same period.

But deaths are only "the tip of the iceberg," said Ollie Jay of the University of Sydney's Heat and Health Research Center. "Except that iceberg is not melting, it's growing every year." Beneath the surface are also heatstroke, lost sleep, and worsening chronic health conditions.

The economic harms are mounting too. Working in extreme heat puts people at risk of heat exhaustion, illness or injury and, ultimately, losing income and livelihoods.

Heat wiped out 573 billion potential working hours in 2025, with farmworkers bearing the brunt. Vulnerable economies in Africa and South-East Asia were hit hardest with losses reaching 5% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the more developed economies.

"The economic toll is battering vulnerable sectors and communities the hardest," Marina Romanello, executive director of the Lancet Countdown, who is based at University College London, told journalists at a press briefing.

Water extremes are intensifying too. Satellite data show that since 2003, 43% of the world's land has been steadily drying out, while 37% has been getting wetter. Together, that is more than 80% of land shifting to extremes that threaten crops, food supplies, and sanitation.

Drought can leave people without safe drinking water and raises the risk of infectious disease, while floods bring drowning, injury and contaminated water.

Heat waves and droughts pushed nearly 128 million more people into food insecurity in 2024, compared with the 1981–2010 average.

"This isn't a gradual worsening; it's a step change," Romanello said.

What would declaring a global health emergency change?

To save lives and protect human health, experts are calling for a new WHO instrument to help countries share information, coordinate responses, monitor threats, and disburse funds. The United Nations and its member states would create the mechanism.

The closest existing version of this is the WHO's Public Health Emergency of International Concern mechanism (PHEIC) used during the COVID-19 pandemic and mpox outbreaks. But built with short-term emergencies in mind, it falls short of addressing a complex threat that requires sustained global action across multiple sectors, like climate change. 

The world needs a broader approach, "so that we're not responding to emergency after emergency," said Romanello. "We're doing a cohesive long-term response that builds resilience, builds capacities and builds the possibilities of countries to avoid further emergencies."

Progress happening but not nearly fast enough

Romanello told journalists that "we have more than enough proof" that such action does improve health outcomes. "Early warning systems informed by climate, have already seen a reduction in the adverse impacts of these extreme weather events," she said.

The growth in renewable energy has also partly aided a reduction in deaths from fossil fuel air pollution in half of 140 countries assessed since 2016, preventing an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

And 56 countries now have national plans to adapt their health services for climate impacts, such as heat waves and disease outbreaks, up from just 14 in 2015.

But progress remains too slow, according to the report.

Fossil fuels, the burning of which releases emissions fueling planetary heating as well as other pollutants, still supply more than 80% of the world's energy.

Energy-related emissions hit a record high in 2024. The world's 100 largest oil and gas companies are on track to produce 150% more oil and gas by 2040 than is compatible with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit). A year ago, that figure was 138%. 

Investing in an old technology

Governments continue to fund fossil fuels, with net subsidies doubling since 2016 to $6.2 trillion. In 2024, 10 countries spent more on such subsidies than on their entire health systems.

Yet as fossil fuel prices rise and renewables become cheaper, these polluting technologies are becoming increasingly uneconomical, said Romanello. 

Romanello likened new fossil fuel investment to "investing in Blockbuster when you have Netflix," — a bet on an old technology, referring to the once ubiquitous video rental store that failed to adapt to streaming.

Meanwhile, money to help health systems adapt to climate change is scarce. Developing countries estimate they need around $3.3 billion a year for such adaptations, which the Lancet authors say is likely an underestimate. Only about a third of that was committed in 2024. Foreign aid reductions, led by the US and followed by Germany, which made the second-largest cut, are widening the gap.

"This report is a stark warning that climate change is a health emergency," said Helen Clark, former prime minister of New Zealand and chair of the Lancet Countdown's board. "What's missing is not evidence, but the political will to act on it."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

entries.title: Egypt orders closure of independent news site Mada Masr
entries.summary: Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained and fined over licensing violations. Rights groups condemned the ruling as a major blow to press freedom in Egypt, where independent media face growing pressure.
entries.content:
October 28, 2026

Editor-in-chief Lina Attalah was briefly detained and fined over licensing violations. Rights groups condemned the ruling as a major blow to press freedom in Egypt, where independent media face growing pressure.

An Egyptian court on Tuesday ordered the closure of independent news website Mada Masr after convicting its editor-in-chief, Lina Attalah, of operating without a license.

Attalah, one of Egypt's most prominent journalists, was detained for several hours following the verdict before being released after paying a fine.

The court imposed a fine of 3 million Egyptian pounds (around $53,400; €48,112), the maximum penalty for the offense. It also ordered the website to shut down and its equipment to be confiscated.

Mada Masr, founded in 2013, is one of Egypt's few remaining independent news outlets. It is known for investigating corruption, human rights violations and the military's powerful role in the country.

What happened during Lina Attalah's trial?

Attalah's lawyers said the court rejected their requests to review the case file and submit additional evidence during Tuesday's hearing in Cairo.

According to Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the hearing, the judge then appointed a new lawyer to represent Attalah despite objections from her eight-person defense team.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer, who had not uttered a single word, and entered them into the official record," Bahgat told news agency AFP.

The judge announced the verdict amid protests from the defense before security officers detained Attalah.

She was released after Mada Masr paid the fine, her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari confirmed. The outlet plans to appeal the closure order.

During her release procedures, Attalah also learned that she had been sentenced in absentia in a separate case in 2024 to one year in prison and a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds.

That conviction concerned charges of spreading false news and operating an unlicensed website. Her lawyers have challenged the ruling, with a new hearing scheduled for November 11.

Why has Egypt targeted Mada Masr?

Mada Masr has faced years of legal battles with Egyptian authorities, who have blocked access to its website inside the country since 2017.

The outlet says it first applied for a license in 2018 but received no response. It only learned that its application had been rejected when prosecutors raised the issue during another case in 2022.

Mada Masr challenged that decision and says its latest application has been awaiting a response since 2023.

Six cases have been brought against the outlet and its journalists over the past six years, but Tuesday's trial was the first of its kind.

Egyptian authorities maintain that the country respects freedom of expression but insist that media organizations must comply with the law, protect national security and counter misinformation.

How have press freedom groups reacted?

The ruling drew widespread international condemnation.

A coalition of 119 rights organizations and media outlets, including Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), described the prosecution as an "unprecedented attack on press freedom."

"Today's decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said.

Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called the ruling "outrageous" and "shameful."

"If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe," said CPJ regional director Sara Qudah.

US Senator Chris Van Hollen also criticized the prosecution, describing the charges as baseless and saying that "journalism is not a crime."

What is the state of press freedom in Egypt?

The case comes amid a broader crackdown on independent journalism.

Six journalists from the fact-checking platform Matsadaash were arrested in September and subsequently charged with terrorism-related offenses.

Authorities accuse them of links to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood and spreading false information to undermine confidence in state institutions and encourage protests.

The journalists have reported being tortured following their arrests, according to EIPR. Egypt's Interior Ministry has denied the allegations.

On Tuesday, prosecutors extended their pretrial detention by another 15 days. Rights groups warn that such detention can continue for months or even years.

According to EIPR, Egypt currently holds 26 journalists in connection with their work.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

entries.title: Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US amid investigation — reports
entries.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro is on the way to the US, according to reports citing people close to the senator. The US State Department said it will issue visas to the senator and his family.
entries.content:
Brazil

Flavio Bolsonaro flees Brazil for US amid investigation — reports

October 27, 2026

Flavio Bolsonaro is on the way to the US, according to reports citing people close to the senator. The US State Department said it will issue visas to the senator and his family.

Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after he was defeated in Sunday's presidential election, Folha de S.Paulo and Reuters reported, citing sources close to the senator.

The US State Department will issue visas to Flavio Bolsonaro and his family to allow them to enter the US, a senior State Department official told Reuters and other news agencies.

Leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who secured the runoff victory in elections, told supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had left the country, but he didn't have information about Bolsonaro's exact whereabouts.

Brazil is "the second country" of the Bolsonaro family, Lula added.

"The first is licking American boots," the reelected president said. "Those who are not liable do not fear. A fellow that secretly leaves his country, that's because he is liable for something."

Bolsonaro wasn't allowed to leave Brazil

The Supreme Court had asked Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, to surrender his passports to stop him from leaving the country amid investigations into the senator.

It was reported that Bolsonaro had refused to comply with the order, although other reports contradicted this.

The AFP news agency cited a police official as saying that Bolsonaro's passports had been cancelled and there was no official record of him leaving the country.

Brazilian newspaper Folha de S.Paulo reported that Bolsonaro's plane was scheduled to land in either Miami or Dallas.

How did Bolsonaro exit Brazil?

Argentine news outlet Infobae reported earlier today that Bolsonaro had crossed into Argentina to board a plane to the US.

A spokesperson for Argentina's Ministry of Security denied the reports that the conservative Brazilian senator had entered the country.

Brazilian media reports earlier said that the federal police were still searching for him.

Bolsonaro leaves Brazil after losing presidential election: What to know

Bolsonaro lost Brazil's presidential election runoff on Sunday after an incredibly tight voting count through the evening until his challenger, Lula, surged ahead.

Bolsonaro had initially said he would seek to annul the election results, citing alleged irregularities.But Bolsonaro's Liberal Party on Tuesday acknowledged the results.

In a video on Instagram on Monday, Bolsonaro said he had been served with a Supreme Court order to hand over his passports so he couldn't leave the country.

He had said he was planning to hand over his passports, but reports on Tuesday said the deadline had passed leading to their cancellation.

What are the investigations against Flavio Bolsonaro about?

The senator has been accused of laundering money through a sports betting company, money that was deducted from government pensions to senior citizens.

A second investigation is looking into Bolsonaro's connections to a disgraced banker from whom he allegedly accepted millions of dollars to finance the biopic about his father, titled "Dark Horse."

Bolsonaro loses his immunity from prosecution once his Senate term comes to end in February 2027. He has denied wrongdoing in both cases.

Bolsonaro asked to surrender passports: What to know

Bolsonaro said that he had received the Supreme Court order outside the home where his father, Jair Bolsonaro, is under house arrest.

He said the order was issued by Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same judge who sentenced his father to prison.

He also pointed to comments made by his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who said on a podcast last week that his sibling should leave the country if he lost the election.

Eduardo, who lives in the US, was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration. He was sentenced to four years in prison and a warrant was issued for his arrest.

Edited by: Alex Berry and Wesley Dockery

entries.title: EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers
entries.summary: The European Commission has unveiled a new plan to give Frontex more resources to ensure the return of irregular migrants, including by supporting non-EU countries. The move comes after the tragedy in Ceuta.
entries.content:
Europe

EU proposes giving Frontex border agency new major powers

October 27, 2026

The European Commission has unveiled a new plan to give Frontex more resources to ensure the return of irregular migrants, including by supporting non-EU countries. The move comes after the tragedy in Ceuta.

The European Commission on Tuesdayunveiled a new proposal to beef up the powers of the EU border agency in order to empower it to support the return of irregular migrants.

The proposed legislation gives the agency, called Frontex, more resources to act beyond EU territory.

The plan would give the agency the power to support non-EU countries to return migrants to their countries of origin.

The proposal comes as EU member states increasingly focus on returns, saying too many people who are asked to leave the bloc remain.

EU border agency to be beefed up after Ceuta humanitarian crisis of summer

The new role for Frontex comes after the humanitarian crisis in Ceuta this summer.

The tragedy in the Spanish exclave was seized upon by some EU member states as an example of where the EU could do more to block people from reaching the EU.

Italy, for example, placed some temporary border controls on travel from Spain.

Spain's prime minister at the time criticized several EU member states for their "selfish" response to the influx of migrants to Ceuta.

"Today we propose that Frontex becomes the central EU actor on returns," Magnus Brunner, commissioner for internal affairs ​and migration, told reporters.

"It will be able to act faster, with a quick reaction force that can ⁠deploy within ⁠24 hours and spot risks ⁠early, before an ​event becomes a crisis," Brunner added.

Frontex to be given wide powers to support deportation of irregular migrants

The ability to deport migrants from non-EU countries means that Frontex could, for instance, deport a Bangladeshi national from Libya, where many migrants start the final leg of their journey into the bloc.

The plan envisages gradually expanding Frontex's standing corps to 30,000 officers by creating a new "European border and return reserve" of 17,000 officers within the next 15 years.

Those officers would remain at the disposal of member states and could be deployed when needed, the commission said in a statement.

The proposal would also create a new EU Return Coordination Center within Frontex and expand the agency's role across the entire deportation process.

It would also include a new online monitoring center to track border-related developments on social media and support action against content linked to border security risks.

Frontex reform criticized by rights groups

Frontex has been responsible for guarding the external borders of the EU as well as ensuring the rights of new arrivals.

It has been criticized for its lack of accountability in the past.

The planned reform shrinks the scope of the agency's internal rights watchdog, with complaints to be referred to national authorities.

"The Commission is pandering to populism and the far right on migration," said Tineke Strik, a Dutch MEP from the Greens/EFA group.

"We need a human rights-based approach to border management and Frontex plays a key role. But instead the Commission ​risks turning Frontex into a European version of ICE," she said.

Edited: Alex Berry

entries.title: Mbappe apologizes as Chinese sponsors drop him and TV broadcasts are halted over Mao dictator remark
entries.summary: French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

French soccer star Kylian Mbappe has apologized after apparently referring to Mao Zedong as a dictator. Chinese sponsors have dropped him, while state television has suspended Spanish league broadcasts.

France striker Kylian Mbappe apologized after apparently referring to China's founding leader Mao Zedong as a dictator in a video that circulated online.

The controversy prompted three major Chinese companies to sever sponsorship ties with the Real Madrid forward, while Chinese state television suspended broadcasts of Spain's La Liga.

What did Mbappe say about Mao?

The controversy began when a video circulated showing Mbappe discussing his favorite internet meme featuring himself.

In the clip, apparently filmed ahead of an appearance on the French online talk show The Bridge, Mbappe referred to an image depicting his face superimposed on the body of "some guy ... I think he's a Chinese dictator."

The image appeared to depict Mao Zedong, who founded the People's Republic of China in 1949 and ruled until his death in 1976. Jokes about country's former leader and descriptions of him as a dictator remain taboo.

Mbappe has previously been depicted as authoritarian leaders in online memes mocking his perceived influence over teammates and suggestions that he has the power to influence club decisions.

Mbappe has been nicknamed "the dictator" in the European press.

How did Mbappe apologize?

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," Mbappe said in a statement.

"I apologize to everyone my words have upset. This was absolutely not my intention. I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry."

Chinese sponsors cut ties with Mbappe

Chinese beverage company Dongpeng, dairy producer Mengniu and cheesemaker Milkground announced they were ending their partnerships with the French international.

In similarly worded statements, each said that they oppose "any words and actions that hurt national sentiment."

China Media Group, which oversees state broadcaster CCTV, also suspended broadcasts of La Liga matches and removed advertisements featuring Mbappe.

La Liga apologized for the controversy, saying Mbappe's comments were made in a personal capacity and did not represent the Spanish league.

Chinese state broadcaster CCTV subsequently said it would consider Mbappe's apology but would also judge his future actions.

In response to a question about the controversy, China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun said that "words and actions that hurt the feelings of the Chinese people will naturally be met with joint opposition from all sectors of Chinese society."

Why is Mao such a sensitive subject in China?

Mao remains a revered figure in China, where public criticism of the former Communist leader is politically sensitive.

His rule was also marked by disastrous political campaigns, including the Great Leap Forward, which contributed to a famine that killed tens of millions of people.

The ruling Communist Party acknowledges some of his mistakes but maintains that his achievements outweighed them, making criticism of his legacy politically sensitive.

Edited by: Alex Berry

If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

entries.title: Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?
entries.summary: With the US reopening talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, and several Southeast Asian countries restarting diplomatic contacts, the EU is facing uncomfortable questions about its own boycott of the junta.
entries.content:
Myanmar

Myanmar: Is the US undermining the EU's diplomatic blockade?

October 27, 2026

With the US reopening talks with Myanmar's military-backed government, and several Southeast Asian countries restarting diplomatic contacts, the EU is facing uncomfortable questions about its own boycott of the junta.

The US government has begun a quiet reproachment with Myanmar's military-backed government, holding two rounds of talks since September with State Department representative Michael Vance. American diplomats reportedly meet Myanmar officials in Naypyitaw and then in Tokyo earlier this month.

Washington wants to tackle online scam centers, secure the release of imprisoned American businessman Adam Castillo, and potentially gain access to Myanmar's rare-earth resources. The market for the valuable minerals is currently controlled by the US rival China.

Meanwhile, Southeast Asian governments are also increasingly questioning their policy of isolating Myanmar's military leadership. Multiple countries have already renewed direct diplomatic contacts.

The EU, however, continues to reject the legitimacy of the military junta in the war-torn country. The European bloc has also remained unmoved by the 2025/2026 election, which ended with military chief Min Aung Hlaing becoming the president. The military retains control over the political system.

EU's sanctions still in force

The EU responded to Myanmar's February 2021 military coup by suspending direct financial assistance to the government, imposing targeted sanctions and sharply reducing diplomatic engagement with the military authorities.

Its sanctions currently cover 105 individuals and 22 entities connected to the military. In April, the EU extended these measures for another 12 months.

At the same time, Brussels is providing humanitarian assistance to displaced communities and Rohingya refugees and is supporting civil society organizations.

The EU also stopped short of withdrawing Myanmar's preferential trade access because of concerns about the consequences for workers, particularly the mostly young women employed in the country's garment industry. Last year, bilateral goods trade was worth about €4 billion ($4.46 billion), up from €3.4 billion in 2019.

Brussels supports ASEAN's peace deal

The civil war triggered by the 2021 coup has killed an estimated 100,000 people. Rebel groups still control or contest large swathes of Myanmar, and over 4 million people have been internally displaced, according to UN data.

The EU "continues to uphold its policy of non-recognition of the current military regime," in view of "the ongoing violence and the attack against its own population," an EU spokesman told DW.

At the same time, the bloc "is closely monitoring developments in the discussions and positions of the United States, Japan, ASEAN countries and other major actors with representatives of Myanmar's military regime."

"It also supports ASEAN efforts, in particular the Five-Point Consensus, which has yet to be fully implemented," the spokesperson added, referring to the peace deal proposed by the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in 2021.

Myanmar diplomats reach out to European partners

In the aftermath of the coup, ASEAN took the unprecedented decision to exclude Myanmar's military leaders from its highest-level meetings after the junta failed to implement the regional peace plan.

However, ASEAN's position is showing signs of change. Some member states, most notably Myanmar's neighbor Thailand, signal growing frustration with the lack of progress towards ending Myanmar's civil war.

Last week, Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow welcomed Washington's renewed engagement and suggested that ASEAN members would hold substantive discussions about Myanmar's future at their summit in Manila next month.

Myanmar's authorities are also seeking to break their diplomatic isolation. In September, Myanmar's leader Hlaing gave an interview to Time magazine, his first with a major Western publication since the coup, as part of an apparent effort to rebuild relations with Western governments.

On October 22, Burma Campaign UK, a London-based human rights organization, accused the British government of making a "significant shift in approach" after the British Foreign Office hosted Win Zeyar Tun, the charge d'affaires of Myanmar's military-controlled embassy in London, at an ASEAN diplomatic gathering days earlier.

According to an article published by Intelligence Online this month, the regime's charge d'affaires in Brussels, Khin Thidar Ay, has also sought contacts with European politicians, including Czech MEP Ondrej Dostal, a member of the European Parliament's delegation for Southeast Asia.

EU's isolation 'has achieved relatively little'

Kristina Kironska, of Palacky University Olomouc in the Czech Republic and an expert on the EU's policy on Myanmar, told DW that the EU has little reason to follow Washington's apparent shift towards engagement with the Myanmar junta.

The US strategy "appears to be pursuing specific interests" such as rare earth mining and cybercrime, she said.

However, the most important rare earth mining operations are no longer controlled by the military, but by rebels such as the Kachin Independence Organization in Kachin State. "It remains to be seen what the US can achieve through negotiations with the junta," she said.

The EU has long positioned itself as a defender of democracy and human rights in Myanmar, "so abandoning this now because the US is exploring a new, perhaps more transactional approach would undermine the EU's credibility," Kironska added.

"At the same time, isolation has achieved relatively little. The question is therefore not whether the EU should engage, but rather with whom and under what conditions."

Balancing act between Myanmar's rebels and junta

The EU is forced to consider risks to its own influence. If Washington, ASEAN governments and other regional powers increase their engagement with Myanmar's authorities, the EU risks becoming increasingly marginal in discussions about the country's political future.

Yet greater engagement with the military could undermine Brussels' relations with Myanmar's democratic opposition and ethnic resistance organizations, many of which control substantial territory.

"The key question for Brussels is whether it can remain a credible defender of democratic change while ensuring that it still has a meaningful voice in the negotiations that will determine Myanmar's future," Sabe Soe, director of the NGO Burma Centre Prague, told DW.

One possibility is for Brussels to maintain its sanctions against military leaders and their businesses while expanding diplomacy through ASEAN, the UN and other regional partners. The EU could also tie any easing of restrictions to humanitarian access, improvements in political freedoms and progress towards peace.

Soe also suggested that the EU could pursue economic engagement in areas administered by revolutionary and ethnic resistance forces, offering an alternative to engagement centred on the military authorities in Naypyidaw.

This approach would allow the EU to remain involved in Myanmar's future without necessarily recognizing its military-backed government, she said.

For now, Brussels seems to have little appetite for a fundamental policy rethink. But this could change as more governments reopen their doors to Myanmar's generals.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Harry Kane: Ballon d’Or for Bayern Munich striker
entries.summary: Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.
entries.content:
October 27, 2026

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane has won football's most prestigious individual prize, beating Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal. Kane has developed even more in the Bundesliga despite an uneven league.

To most Bayern Munich fans under the age of 40, Karl-Heinz Rummenigge was the club CEO who regularly spoke his mind. Fans with longer memories, or a better grasp of Bavarian football history, recall Rummenigge as one of the club's all-time great players. He was also the last Bayern man to win the Ballon d'Or — in 1981. The last Bundesliga player to win was Borussia Dortmund's Matthias Sammer, in 1996.

That long drought ended on Monday, with Harry Kane, born 12 years after Rummenigge's win, picking up the 2026 trophy at a ceremony held, as a one-off, in his native London.

"I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he said on stage.

Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane later told British sports streaming plaftorm DAZN.

Lamine Yamal, the prodigious Barcelona and Spain forward who won the Euros at 16, finished third. At the end of the 2025-26 season, on which the award is judged, Yamal won the World Cup with Spain as well as the La Liga title. Kylian Mbappe came in second.

Kane's career not just measured in numbers

Kane's 73 goals for club and country last season made for a strong case, and the Bundesliga's most expensive signing of all time has already racked up 156 goals in 159 games for the serial German champions. But it's not just the numbers that tell the story, according to his club coach.

"People in England saw him as a goalscorer during his time playing there," Vincent Kompany said of Kane last season. "We've seen other qualities too, such as his footballing intelligence. We can appreciate that now — it was perhaps somewhat underestimated in England. He's like a fine wine that improves with age. I also enjoy that aspect of his game."

Kane continues to improve at 33, a point when many footballers start to regress. Though he is helped by being more reliant on guile and technique than pace, Kane's professionalism is key to staying at the top, according to his Bayern teammate Serge Gnabry.

"He always has the right attitude, always leads the way and sets the tone," Gnabry said ahead of Bayern's 2-2 draw in the Champions League against Arsenal last week. "He never strays from his path, helps the team with his performance and is a top-tier player."

Kane scored a penalty in that match and provided a sensational pass from which Alphonso Davies scored Bayern's opener, another reminder of his all-round game. "The pass was one of my best ones," Kane said after the match. "I knew Phonzy [Davies] would be able to get there with his speed. Whatever I can do to help the team, I'll do. At the moment, it seems to be with assists more than goals."

Kane's 'greatest strength'

That attitude has been with Kane from the start. His first-ever coach, Dave Bricknell, from Ridgeway Rovers, an amateur club in northeast London, told DW after Kane joined Bayern from Spurs in 2023: "Harry's mentality is his greatest strength. He doesn't let anything worry him. If he misses a chance, he doesn't care — he will go and score from another chance."

His England coach, Thomas Tuchel, has also emphasized Kane's leadership. "He is the first one to push everyone, and that is his mindset, and he became a very, very hardworking forward on top of his finishing skills, Tuchel said in September as Kane extended his England goal-scoring record against the Czech Republic. "He is a complete package."

There are detractors who point to perceived "stat-padding," or scoring against inferior opponents in international qualifiers and in the Bundesliga, where there are fewer elite teams and a lot less money, than in England. Though Kane's ratio of 213 goals in 320 games in the Premier League is a little off his Bundesliga stats, it bears comparison with any other player in the history of the league.

Kane winning the award is also a boost in profile for the Bundesliga, which has been unable to keep pace, both commercially and on the pitch, with other top European leagues of late, particularly the Premier League and La Liga.

Winning it in a league outside of England or Spain perhaps makes Kane's feat even greater. Other than Ousmane Dembele, who won it last year after Paris Saint-Germain's Champions League win, and Lionel Messi, a serial Ballon d'Or winner, the last player to take the Ballon d'Or for a season played outside England or Spain was was Kaka at AC Milan in 2007, when Italy's Serie A was considered a stronger league.

Kane's career hasn't been straightforward, something he admitted in his speech. After signing his first senior contract with Spurs in July 2010, he was sent out on various loans to lower league sides between 2011-2013 without ever making a huge impression.

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs, I had a lot of loan moves, I had to fight my way to be the very best right now, and I hope that can give you determination as well," Kane said in his speech.

Domestic trophies won but international success eludes

For former teammate Jermain Defoe, who also coached Kane at Spurs, those experiences were formative.

"You have to show a resilience. It's not easy when you go out on loan, it can feel like you're being rejected by the club that you are at, which isn't the case," he told DW in 2023, before adding that Kane's ability was always clear.

"When he joined up with the [Tottenham] first team, you could see the potential," Defoe said. "He was always a good finisher, always hit the ball clean. … With Harry you already knew, he had that natural instinct and always felt comfortable in front of goal."

Those goals have, after a failure to win a trophy in England, led to two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup. But success with England remains elusive after a 2026 World Cup exit in the semifinals. Kane will be 35 by the time of the next Euros, in the UK and Ireland in 2028, and has a deal with Bayern until the following year. His form since joining Bayern suggests that he could get better still.

Edited by: Jonathan Harding

This article was first published on October 22, 2026. It was updated on October 27 after Harry Kane won the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

entries.title: Will elections in Israel change its Iran approach?
entries.summary: As Israelis head to the polls, the country's conflict with Iran casts a long shadow over the ballot box. But any leadership changes in Israel may not be enough to shake up its grand strategy on Tehran.
entries.content:
Asia

Will elections in Israel change its Iran approach?

October 27, 2026

As Israelis head to the polls, the country's conflict with Iran casts a long shadow over the ballot box. But any leadership changes in Israel may not be enough to shake up its grand strategy on Tehran.

Israel's vote this Tuesday is the first general election for the country since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023 — an assault which led to one of the deepest security crises in Israel's history.

As incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu fights to retain power, the question is not merely who will lead Israel's next government, but also how that government will navigate the region-wide security crisis that was triggered by the attack and the Israeli reaction, which included launching a war against Iran.

US President Donald Trump recently issued a full-throated endorsement of the incumbent Israeli leader as a "warrior prime minister" and warned that any other choice would affect Israel's alliance with Washington.

"If Israel has the wrong leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi (Benjamin Netanyahu), America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Trump said in an online post, referring to the Iran conflict.

Behind the scenes, however, media reports indicated a rift between the Israeli government and the Trump administration. According to The Financial Times, the Israeli military intended to launch a new round of attacks on Iran's nuclear facilities, government centers, and energy infrastructure around October 10. However, Trump opposed the new escalation before the US midterm elections on November 3.

The Jerusalem Post later questioned the narrative, reporting that the army had no specific directive for such an operation.

Israel's moves hinge on Trump's decision

The Israeli race has turned into a tight duel between Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot — former IDF (Israel Defense Forces) chief of staff and leader of the front-running centrist party "Yashar."

But Raz Zimmt, the head of the Iran program at the Tel Aviv-based Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), warns political divisions between the two options are not deep enough to speak of a "fundamental change in Tel Aviv's approach toward Tehran" after the election.

"In the perception of Israel's left, right, and center factions regarding the Iranian threat, especially its nuclear threat, there are minor differences," Zimmt told DW.

Moreover, according to Zimmt, any military escalation against Iran depends "on the decision of the US president" far more than on the identity of Israel's prime minister.

"Overall, I do not expect Israel's policy toward Iran and its proxies to undergo dramatic changes, regardless of the future government's composition," he said.

INSS senior fellow Danny Citrinovitch agreed that one should not expect "fundamental changes" in Israel's Iran policy depending on the election outcome.

"Even if Netanyahu personally steps down from power, his influence and the policies shaped over recent years will not simply vanish," Citrinovitch told DW.

Hamas attack as a turning point for Israel and Iran

The current consensus on Iran can be traced to the Hamas terror attack three years ago. Before the assault, according to Navid Toobian from the US-based Middle East Media Research Institute, many believed Israel should deal with the Islamic Republic "in a limited and managed way" and confront only the arms of the so-called "Axis of Resistance." But October 7 completely changed the rules of the game.

While Israel had been aware of Iran's slogans calling for its destruction, it was believed that such calls had an "internal aspect" to rally the base of hardcore Islamists in Iran, Toobian said.

The terror strike by the Iran-allied Hamas, however, showed that Tehran "spares no effort to strike Israel."

What are US and Israel hoping to achieve in the Iran war?

Damon Golriz, a researcher at the Hague Institute for Geopolitics, also points to October 7 as the trigger of the "largest historical trauma of the Jewish nation."

"Preserving Iran's nuclear ambitions and continuous threats against Israel has intensified this fear that for a large portion of Israeli society, today's rulers in Iran have become a symbol of a historical threat," he told DW.

With that in mind, the current US and Israeli policy towards Iran follows three vectors, according to Golriz.

"First, the removal of the regime's leaders; second, industrial and infrastructural collapse," and third, orchestrating a civil war and what he called "geographic scissors" to dismember Iran with the help of armed Kurdish and Baluch separatists, he said.

The US and Israel, however, are not the only players in the conflict. In a recent report, the Reuters news agency cited senior Iranian security officials as saying that Tehran has prepared detailed operational plans for retaliatory strikes. Tehran warned that their retaliatory tools include destroying undersea fiber-optic communication cables in the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz, alongside targeting US-dependent data centers and AI infrastructure in the region.

Diplomacy: A missed opportunity?

Commenting on possible alternatives to military escalation, Golriz highlights a diplomatic opportunity that opened six months ago in Islamabad, when Tehran agreed to never initiate war or military operations against Israel.

"For the first time in the history of the Islamic Republic, the fundamental national security interests of Israel were signed by the presidents of Iran and the United States," according to Gorliz.

The first article of the Islamabad framework could have been "the beginning of the end for 'Death to America' slogans and anti-Jewish threats, including 'Death to Israel," Golriz said.

This diplomatic window was quickly closed, but "with political will, the provisions and spirit of the Islamabad Memorandum will be the first strategic step toward lasting peace," he said.

But INSS senior fellow Citrinovitch was less optimistic when assessing the willingness of Israeli elites to return to diplomacy.

"Currently, returning to the nuclear deal has no place in Israel's political arena," he told DW.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

entries.title: Denmark's Frederiksen criticizes Finland and Norway for calling Putin without coordinating with allies, despite consultation with Ukraine
entries.summary: Finland and Norway have called Putin about ending the Ukraine war, drawing Danish criticism. The dispute highlights divisions over European engagement with Moscow ahead of planned US-led peace talks.
entries.content:
Norway

Denmark criticizes Finnish and Norwegian call with Putin on Ukraine

October 27, 2026

Finland and Norway have called Putin about ending the Ukraine war, drawing Danish criticism. The dispute highlights divisions over European engagement with Moscow ahead of planned US-led peace talks.

Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized Finland's and Norway's leaders Tuesday after they held a joint phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin about ending the war in Ukraine.

The call came ahead of planned US-led peace talks, which European leaders are seeking to join.

Why did Denmark criticize the call?

Frederiksen said that Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store had gone "solo.”

"I'm very sceptical about this Norwegian and Finnish initiative. It hasn't been coordinated with any of the rest of us," she told reporters while attending a meeting of Nordics leaders.

"I honestly don't know what those two countries think they can achieve with this."

"I believe we should keep Europe united, rather than going it alone," Frederiksen said.

Stubb and Store said they had consulted Ukraine before initiating the call.

They stressed that they represented their own countries and were not speaking on behalf of Europe.

What did the leaders discuss with Putin?

Stubb described the conversation as "frank and substantive." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed the call, the first between the three leaders.

"The outcome of this war will have a direct impact on our and the broader European security. Ending the war requires direct discussions," Stubb said.

Finland and Norway both border Russia and have supported Ukraine throughout the war.

Store said the leaders had emphasized de-escalation.

"The war comes with enormous human and material costs. The suffering and destruction will impact generations," he said.

How was Ukraine involved?

The call followed an October 20 meeting in Oslo involving Stubb, Store, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and US envoy Steve Witkoff. US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner joined remotely.

Zelenskyy also spoke with the Nordic leaders after their conversation with Putin.

"Finland and Norway will continue to support Ukraine, and the efforts to find a just and lasting peace," Stubb wrote on social media.

A US-mediated ceasefire ‌in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky is set to last until November 1,

Ukraine's ‌top negotiator Davyd ‌Arakhamia said ‌on Tuesday.

"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," he said on Telegram, adding that every ‌such step brings peace closer.
